summary: This standards-track document defines a unicast-based way to speed up joining a multicast RTP session. A joining receiver may wait for reference information; the unicast burst provides it so playback starts sooner.

plainLanguage.summary:
Joining a multicast channel is slow when the channel sends the information a viewer needs at the start of every cycle, because the viewer has to wait for the next cycle. This RFC makes the server send that information directly to the viewer, unicast, so the viewer can start at once.

The three control messages travel in the feedback channel that RTP already uses, so no new transport is needed.

questions: how to join multicast video faster
what is rams rapid acquisition of multicast rtp sessions
how to speed up iptv channel change
subtitle: Getting a viewer into a multicast channel quickly by sending it the information it needs directly.

tldr.problem: A receiver that joins a multicast session has to wait for the next copy of the reference information the session carries, and for its buffers to fill, so the channel takes a noticeable time to appear.
tldr.mechanism: RAMS adds three control messages to the RTCP feedback channel. The receiver asks the session's feedback target for the reference information, the server sends it over a unicast RTP session, and the receiver then joins the multicast session.
tldr.outcome: A viewer can start playing sooner, which matters for IPTV channel changes. The method reuses the existing RTP retransmission machinery, and the RFC says it must not be used across a best-effort path. The document is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 6285 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It defines the RAMS signalling messages, which ride in the RTCP feedback channel defined in RFC 4585, and it relies on the unicast feedback model of RFC 5760 and the retransmission payload format of RFC 4588.

sections.title: The Problem: Joining a Multicast Session Slowly
sections.content:
Most multicast flows carry a stream of related data. A receiver has to acquire certain information before it can start processing any of that data, and this document calls it Reference Information. It is usually sent periodically in the multicast session, and it typically holds things such as a description of the schema for the rest of the data, references to which data to process, encryption information including keys, and anything else the receiver needs.

Real-time multicast applications need receivers to buffer data: to smooth out network jitter, to allow loss repair such as forward error correction or retransmission to recover missing packets, and to satisfy the application. When a receiver joins a multicast session it has no control over which point in the flow is being sent, so sometimes it joins just before the Reference Information goes past, and sometimes just after, in which case it has to wait for the whole Reference Information to come round again. Other times the Reference Information is not contiguous but spread over a long period, so the receiver waits for all of it.

The total of waiting for the Reference Information and waiting for buffers to fill is what this document calls the Acquisition Delay: the difference between the time the receiver wants to join and the time it has all the Reference Information it needs. It differs from receiver to receiver, and depends on when the receiver joined, how often the Reference Information repeats, how big it is, and on the application and transport.

The varying acquisition delay is a problem for receivers that move between multicast sessions, which is the normal case in IPTV where compressed video streams are multicast in different source-specific multicast sessions and viewers join them at random. This document describes a method that uses the existing tools of RTP and RTCP. Either the multicast source, or the distribution source in a source-specific multicast session, keeps the Reference Information for a while after sending it, or an intermediary network element, called here a Retransmission Server, joins the multicast session, keeps caching the Reference Information as it is sent, and acts as a feedback target for the session.

When a receiver wants to join, instead of simply sending a group management join message, it sends a request to the feedback target asking for the Reference Information. The retransmission server starts a new unicast RTP session and sends the Reference Information over it, and if there is spare bandwidth it may send it faster than its natural rate. As soon as the receiver has the Reference Information, it joins the multicast session and starts processing the data.
sections.plainLanguage: Joining a multicast channel is slow when the channel sends the information a viewer needs at the start of every cycle, because the viewer has to wait for the next cycle. This RFC makes the server send that information directly to the viewer, unicast, so the viewer can start at once.

sections.title: The Terms Used Here
sections.content:
The document uses a set of terms. The primary multicast RTP session is the multicast session the receiver wants to acquire rapidly, and it may carry several RTP streams. The primary multicast streams are the streams carried in that session. The feedback target is the unicast RTCP feedback target of RFC 5760, and FT_Ap denotes a specific one running on a particular address and port. The retransmission server is the RTP and RTCP endpoint that can generate the retransmission packets and the burst streams. A retransmission or burst packet is an RTP packet formatted as in Section 4 of RFC 4588, whose payload holds the retransmission payload header followed by the payload of the original packet. A burst stream is a unicast stream of such packets that lets the receiver acquire the Reference Information of a primary multicast stream quickly; each burst stream is identified by the SSRC that is unique in the primary multicast session, and it uses the same SSRC and CNAME as the primary multicast stream it belongs to.

Reference Information is the set of media content and metadata that is enough for the receiver to start usefully consuming a media stream; what it holds, its format and its size are specific to the application and out of scope. Preamble Information is a more compact form of the whole or a subset of it, sent out of band. A burst RTP session is the unicast RTP session used to send the burst streams and their RTCP messages, and burst RTP session and retransmission RTP session mean the same thing.

The group management protocol is referred to as SFGMP, which covers IGMP version 3 and MLD version 2, though the method does not depend on a particular version of either.
sections.plainLanguage: The document names three parties: the viewer that wants to join, the server that holds the information and sends it, and the feedback target that the viewer's requests go to. In the text these last two are treated as one box.

sections.title: Where the Delay Comes From
sections.content:
In a source-specific multicast delivery system, three things add to the acquisition delay when a receiver switches from one multicast session to another. The first is the multicast-switching delay: leaving the old session and joining the new one. The join and leave are handled by a group management protocol, and the time varies with how close the upstream router is, the state of the multicast tree, the load on the system and the implementation. Current systems give join latencies of usually less than 200 milliseconds. If the receiver was in another session, it must send a Leave message first; leave times are usually smaller than join times, though a lost Leave or Join message increases the delay.

The second is the Reference Information latency: the time it takes to acquire the Reference Information. It depends on how close the receiver's arrival is to the next time the information is sent, on whether it is sent contiguously, and on its size. For flows with little interdependency between the data, this latency is nil. For flows with a high degree of interdependency, such as compressed audio and video, it can be large and a major contributor to the overall delay.

The third is buffering delay, driven by how the application processes the payload. Loss repair methods such as forward error correction and retransmission need receiver-side buffering to work, and many applications also de-jitter the incoming packets before feeding them to the application, which adds more buffering. Applications have their own needs too: a standard video decoder typically needs a certain amount of coded video, sometimes up to a few seconds, in its pre-decoding buffers before it can start decoding.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things make joining slow: the network setting up the new channel, waiting for the next copy of the information the viewer needs, and waiting for enough data to build up before the decoder can start.

sections.title: What the Protocol Must Achieve
sections.content:
Rapid acquisition is an optimisation of a system that has to work whether or not the optimisation is effective, and the RFC sets out two conditions it must respect. A rapid acquisition operation must fail gracefully: the experience must not be significantly worse for trying and failing than for simply joining the multicast session. And it must not cause collateral damage, either to the multicast session being joined or to other sessions sharing the same resources, so it must avoid interfering with a multicast session that other hosts are receiving at the same time, and with other multicast and non-multicast traffic on the same links.

One challenge is that there may be several bandwidth bottlenecks between the receiver and the server. In commercial IPTV, bottlenecks are often in the aggregation network, in the access links and in the subscriber's home network, and some of those links are shared by many subscribers while others serve one. The state of the links also changes over time, and the receiver may know only part of the network. The receiver should be able to signal the bandwidth it believes it can handle, and the server has to be able to rate limit the flow to stay inside the performance envelope it knows about. Both sides have to be able to tell the other about changes in the requested and delivered rates, and the signalling has to survive packet loss with sensible default behaviour.

A second challenge is that for high bitrate video the unicast burst is fast and short, because its purpose is to let the receiver join the multicast quickly and so limit the resources the burst consumes. Such flows do not suit conventional admission control: end-to-end per-flow signalling such as RSVP has too much latency and control overhead, and a TCP-like approach with a three-way handshake and slow start would defeat the purpose by adding many round-trip times.

These lead to the requirements. The protocol must allow a deterministic upper bound on the extra bandwidth used compared with simply joining the multicast session; a reasonable size bound is e times B, where B is the nominal bandwidth of the primary multicast streams and e is an excess-bandwidth coefficient. The total duration of the unicast burst must also be bounded, since a long burst becomes the bandwidth profile of multi-unicast for the whole system. The scheme should minimise, or better eliminate, the overlap between the unicast burst and the primary multicast stream, and also any gap between them, because a gap has to be repaired later or, without repair, the application sees loss.

There is also at least one round-trip time of slop in the control loop, which shows up as the time between the client asking for the burst and the burst description or the first burst packets arriving. For managing and ending the burst there are two approaches: the receiver can adapt to the burst as it arrives and end it with a second control exchange, or the server can decide on its own.
sections.plainLanguage: Two rules govern the whole design. If the fast path fails, the viewer must be no worse off than if it had never tried. And the fast path must not slow down the channel for everyone else, so its extra traffic has to be capped at a known multiple of the channel's own bitrate and last only a bounded time.

sections.title: The Message Flows
sections.content:
The document defines what the retransmission server and the receiver do.

Port mapping setup. The RTP and RTCP ports of the primary multicast session are set in the session description, but the receiver has to choose its own receive ports for the unicast burst session. Because that session only exists after the request has been sent, the receiver must first set up the port mappings between the unicast and the multicast session and send this mapping to the feedback target along with the request, so that the server knows how to reach it.

Request. The receiver sends a rapid acquisition request to the unicast feedback target of the primary multicast session. It contains the receiver's own SSRC and can contain the media sender SSRCs of the streams it is interested in, and it can carry parameters that constrain the burst, such as buffer and bandwidth limits. Before joining, the receiver learns the addresses of the multicast source, the group and the server by some out-of-band means, and if it wants only some of the streams it has to learn their SSRCs the same way and list them in the request.

Response. The server answers with RAMS Information messages that say what it will do. If the request asks for the whole session and the server cannot serve it, it rejects with a collective reject code, and the receiver gives up and joins the multicast session directly. Otherwise it sends a separate message with a 5xx response code for each stream it cannot serve. A reject that reports a transient problem, such as not enough server or network resources, may be retried, following the RTCP timer rules, but a reject that reports a non-transient problem, such as the codes 504, 505 and 506, must not be retried. For each stream it will serve, the server sends a message with a success code, describing the individual burst streams, and the response carries the RTP sequence number of the first packet of the stream so that the receiver can detect missing initial packets. It is recommended that the server repeats these messages, because they can be lost or delayed and the receiver may start receiving packets first.

Unicast burst. For the streams that were accepted, the server starts sending the burst, made of retransmission packets in the unicast session. It may also send preamble information to prime the media decoders, but only in a format the receiver has said it supports.

Updated request. The receiver may send another request with different values for some fields, and the server has to work out whether it is an update to a burst that is already planned or running, or a new request. An improperly formatted request is answered with a 4xx-level code. The receiver then joins the multicast session and, when it no longer needs the burst, sends a RAMS Termination message.
sections.plainLanguage: The steps are: work out the port numbers, ask the server for the information, wait for its answer, receive the information quickly by unicast, join the channel, and tell the server it no longer needs the unicast copy.

sections.title: The RAMS Messages in RTCP
sections.content:
The signalling is carried in RTCP transport-layer feedback messages, and it is the same for every payload format, so any RTP-based multicast application that supports rapid acquisition uses it. The common packet format of RFC 4585 is used: a version and padding bit, a feedback message type, a packet type, a length, the SSRC of the packet sender, the SSRC of the media source, and a variable-length field for the feedback control information.

In the RAMS messages the packet type is 205 and the feedback message type is 6. Individual messages are identified by a sub-field called the sub-feedback message type. Any reserved field SHALL be set to zero and ignored. The RAMS Request is sub-feedback message type 1, the RAMS Information message is 2 and the RAMS Termination message is 3.

The RAMS Request is sent as unicast feedback in the primary multicast session, and it asks for the rapid acquisition of a primary multicast session or of one or more of its streams. The receiver sets both the packet sender and the media sender SSRC fields to its own SSRC, because the media sender SSRC may not be known yet, and it asks for particular streams through an explicit field, so that it is less likely to ask for the wrong one. The feedback control information of a request holds one RAMS Request, with the requested media sender SSRCs and any optional fields encoded as type-length-value elements.

The extensions use a type-length-value format with a one-octet type, a reserved octet, a two-octet length that does not include the padding needed for alignment, and a variable-size value. If an element does not fall on a 32-bit boundary, the last word is padded with zeros. Extensions go after the mandatory fields, a message must not carry two elements with the same type, and a receiver that does not understand an extension MUST ignore it. Types from 128 to 254 are reserved for private use by vendors, and those carry the vendor's enterprise number so that two vendors cannot collide.
sections.plainLanguage: The three control messages ride in the same feedback channel that RTP already uses for reporting lost packets, so no new transport is needed. A message has a type number and a list of optional fields, each with a length and a value.

sections.title: SDP Signalling
sections.content:
The session description tells the receiver the addresses and ports it needs, and it carries the information about the feedback target and the retransmission stream. The support for ordinary retransmission is signalled with the rtcp-fb line carrying nack, and the support for rapid acquisition with the same line carrying nack rai. When rapid acquisition is enabled, the rtx-time parameter does not mean what it normally means: instead of the time a packet is kept for retransmission measured from its timestamp, it says the time in milliseconds that the server keeps an RTP packet in its cache, measured from the time the packet was received.

The session description lists the SSRC and the CNAME of the primary multicast streams. A receiver that wants only part of a session has to learn the SSRC values from the session description, because it has not yet received any packets, and the CNAME has to be there as well. Listing the SSRC values causes no problem when two senders use the same value in a source-specific multicast session, because a receiver that sees a collision changes its own SSRC, following the rules of RFC 3550.
sections.plainLanguage: The session description says where the channel is and where the server is, and it tells the receiver whether the fast path is available. It also lists which streams are in the channel, so that a receiver can ask for one of them by name.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Applications using RAMS lean on the unicast feedback mechanism of RFC 5760, the payload format of RFC 4588 and the port mapping solution of RFC 6284, so they inherit the security considerations of those documents, and the threats discussed in RFC 5760 need careful thought. Adequate security measures are RECOMMENDED to protect the integrity and authenticity of the session descriptions, so that the transport addresses of the media senders, the distribution sources and the feedback targets are protected.

A RAMS Request can trigger a whole new burst stream, and that stream can contain many retransmission packets sent faster than the nominal rate, so it uses more resources on the server, the receiver and the network. That makes denial of service attacks more intense than attacks on an ordinary retransmission session.

Because the RAMS messages are RTCP messages, steps should be taken to stop tampered or spoofed RTCP packets. A tampered request can trigger an inappropriate burst or alter one that is running: if the maximum receive bitrate in it is changed, the burst can overflow the receiver's buffer or slow down until it is useless. A tampered termination message can stop a valid burst early, leaving gaps in the received packets. A tampered information message can make the receiver take the wrong decisions, and the acquisition can fail.

An RTCP BYE message can also stop a burst, and it is bound to the burst by the receiver's CNAME, so care is needed if CNAMEs are easy to guess and off-path attacks are possible. The server has to judge whether the values in a request are reasonable: a request for many seconds of buffer fill is likely an attempt to prolong a denial of service attack, and a very large maximum receive bitrate is likely an attempt to make the server burst at a rate the network cannot carry. The receiver has to judge the values in the response too: if the burst packets stop arriving while the join time is still far in the future, that may be a sign that someone has tampered with the message.

Source address validation is a basic mitigation against tampered messages, and most of these attacks are prevented by the integrity and authenticity checks of Secure RTP. An attack can still be mounted by legitimate endpoints that send several valid requests to the same feedback target in a synchronised way, so the server needs to limit the rate at which it accepts them.
sections.plainLanguage: The risk is that someone forges a control message and makes the server send a flood of unicast traffic, or makes the receiver give up at the wrong moment. Checking the source of the packets and protecting the RTCP channel with SRTP stops most of it.

messages.label: RAMS-I response
messages.note: Says which streams will be served, and the first sequence number of each.

messages.note: The receiver no longer needs the unicast copy.

viz.caption: THE THREE PARTS OF THE ACQUISITION DELAY

cells: The join and leave handled by the group management protocol
The wait for the next copy of the information the receiver needs
Can be large when the stream is interdependent
Waiting for data to build up, for loss repair and for the decoder
Up to a few seconds of coded video

viz.caption: THE RULES THE DESIGN HAS TO FOLLOW

items.title: Fail gracefully
items.text: A failed rapid acquisition must not be worse than simply joining the multicast session.

items.title: No collateral damage
items.text: The burst must not disturb the multicast session or other traffic sharing the links.

items.title: Bounded extra bandwidth
items.text: At most e times B, where B is the nominal bandwidth of the primary multicast streams.

items.title: Bounded burst duration
items.text: A long burst would become multi-unicast for the whole system.

items.title: Little overlap
items.text: The burst should not run at the same time as the multicast stream it is replacing.

items.title: No gap
items.text: Any gap between the burst and the multicast stream has to be repaired later.

items.label: RAMS Request
items.desc: The receiver asks for the rapid acquisition of a session or of some of its streams.

items.label: RAMS Information
items.desc: The server says what it will send and with which response code.

items.label: RAMS Termination
items.desc: The receiver says the burst is no longer needed.
